claims.text: An enamel-inspired MPEA microstructure can contain nanoscale BCC and FCC phases stabilized at phase boundaries.
The stabilized nanoscale BCC/FCC boundary architecture provides plastic space for dislocation-mediated deformation.
The architecture enables continuous dislocation transfer across phase boundaries.
The stabilized boundaries enable semi-atomic-plane migration.
Dislocation migration through the dual-phase architecture distributes or dissipates strain energy.
The enamel-inspired architecture mitigates strain localization and combines crack deflection, blocking, and bridging toughening mechanisms.
Mitigating strain localization through this architecture retains or enhances toughness.
Reduced phase-boundary stability hinders dislocation mobility.
Interrupted dislocation flow causes strain localization, crack initiation, and reduced toughness.
A targeted thermal treatment or alloying modification can destabilize the phase boundaries and diminish the dual-phase architecture.
Relative to the stable dual-phase baseline, destabilizing the phase boundaries will lower ductility and strain-to-failure.
Destabilizing the phase boundaries will cause earlier crack initiation along phase boundaries.
MPEA failure often involves strain localization along phase or grain boundaries followed by crack initiation.
The optimized architecture exhibits an ultra-high tensile strength of approximately 1458 MPa and ductility of approximately 21%.
Rapid solidification can produce the specified enamel-inspired nanoscale BCC/FCC boundary architecture.
The proposed governing behavior applies under high-strain-rate loading.
The hypothesis is limited to rapidly solidified MPEAs in which the nanoscale BCC/FCC structure is reliably achieved.
The mechanism may not apply to alloys containing significant secondary phases or entirely different microstructures.
